The Last Stop in the Gallery
🎬
Teacher recording notes: Welcome back. Make this feel like a big moment: "This is the LAST lesson in our North America and Caribbean Gallery. You've come a long way — countries, features, landmarks, climate, resources, cultures, settlement. Today is the final comparison." Read the Curator's Question aloud: "What makes Canada, the United States, Mexico, and the Caribbean culturally distinct from one another — and what connects them?" Spotlight courtesy: each region is described on its own terms, never ranked. Tease the badge: "Finish today, and you earn the Regional Observer badge." Under 2 minutes.
🏛️ Virtue Spotlight: Courtesy
Comparing regions is tricky. It's easy to slip into ranking: "this region is better than that one." Courtesy means describing each region on its own terms. Hockey isn't better than baseball. Salsa music isn't better than country music. Each one is true to its place. A good comparison shows the differences AND the shared connections.
🕯️

Your Role Today: You are a Regional Curator, on your last gallery task. Today, you'll match cultural characteristics to the right region and write a comparison panel that helps visitors see both how the regions differ and how they connect.

🔍 TEACHING · EXPLORE
Four Regions, Side by Side
🎬
Teacher recording notes: Walk students through each panel. Canada: two official languages (English & French), parliament government, hockey is the national winter sport, maple leaf as national symbol. United States: English most spoken, many cultures from around the world live together, the Stars and Stripes flag, baseball, jazz and country music. Mexico: Spanish is most spoken, Maya/Aztec heritage still alive, Day of the Dead, mariachi music, foods like tortillas and tamales. Caribbean: many islands speaking Spanish, English, French, Dutch, Creole; reggae, calypso, salsa; African and Indigenous Taíno heritage; sugarcane, beaches, sailing. Emphasize: each region is distinct, but they share a continent, and many cultures cross from one region into another. 3–5 minutes.
1
Learn the Story
📖
Four Regional Panels
What makes each part of the region distinct

This region, North America and the Caribbean, is made up of four big areas. Each one has its own mix of languages, traditions, foods, music, and symbols. Let's walk past each panel.

🍁 Canada is huge. It is the second-largest country in the world. It has two official languages: English and French. Canada is governed by a parliament, and its leader is called the Prime Minister. Hockey is the national winter sport. The red maple leaf on the flag stands for the maple trees that grow across the country, and for the maple syrup that comes from them.

🦅 The United States is a mix of many cultures from many parts of the world. English is spoken most, but you'll also hear Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese, Arabic, and many more languages every day. The flag, the Stars and Stripes, has 50 stars for the 50 states. Baseball is called the national pastime. Jazz, blues, and country music all started in the United States and traveled around the world.

🌶️ Mexico blends Indigenous heritage (Maya, Aztec, and many others) with Spanish heritage from long ago, when Spain ruled Mexico. Spanish is spoken most, but millions of people also speak Indigenous languages like Nahuatl and Maya. The Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos) honors family members who have died. Mariachi music, with trumpets, violins, and guitars, is Mexico's national sound. Tortillas, tamales, and chocolate all come from Mexico.

🏝️ The Caribbean is made up of many islands, each with its own culture. Long ago, Spain, Britain, France, and the Netherlands each ruled different islands. That is why different islands speak different languages: Spanish in Cuba and the Dominican Republic, English in Jamaica and the Bahamas, French in Haiti, Dutch on islands like Curaçao, and Creole languages that blend them. Reggae and calypso music started in the Caribbean, and salsa grew from Cuban music. All three shaped music around the world. The islands share a warm climate, sandy beaches, and a heritage that blends African, Indigenous Taíno, and European cultures.

Even though each place is distinct, they connect in many ways. They share the same continent. Many Indigenous peoples have homelands that cross today's borders. People have traded with each other for hundreds of years. A song from one place often shows up in another, and a food from one place travels to the others.

🤔

Pause & Think: A jazz song born in New Orleans might be played in Toronto, Mexico City, and Havana, all in the same week. What does that tell you about how regions are connected, even though they're different?

3
Match the Characteristics
🎭
Hang the Panels
Tap each card, then tap the region it belongs to.

Eight cultural characteristics. Four regional panels. Read each card and tap the region where it best fits.

Two official languages, English and French: spoken side by side in this country's government, schools, and signs.
The Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos): a colorful holiday in early November when families honor relatives who have passed on.
Reggae and calypso music: musical styles born on the islands, with roots in African and local traditions, that spread around the world.
The Stars and Stripes flag with 50 stars: one star for each of the 50 states that make up the country.
Hockey as the national winter sport: played outdoors on frozen ponds and indoors in arenas across this snowy country.
Mariachi music with trumpets, violins, and guitars: a beloved national sound, often played at weddings, birthdays, and big celebrations.
Many islands with many languages: Spanish, English, French, Dutch, and several Creole languages are all spoken across this group of islands.
Baseball as the national pastime: a summer sport with leagues, hot dogs at the park, and a World Series every fall.
🎉 Gallery complete!
🔎 Discovery Fact: Baseball is loved in the United States, but it's also huge in Mexico, Cuba, and the Dominican Republic. Many players in the U.S. major leagues come from the Dominican Republic, Cuba, and other islands. Cultural characteristics belong to a region, but they also travel between regions.
⏳

Then & Now: Hundreds of years ago, these four regional areas were already culturally distinct, with different languages, different music, and different ways of life. Today, with the internet and travel, cultures share more than ever. Mariachi songs play in Toronto. Hockey is played in Florida. Reggae fills cafés in Mexico City. The regions are still distinct, but the connections are stronger than ever.

···
4
Connect the Ideas
🏷️ Exhibit Label

North America and the Caribbean is made of four regional areas: Canada, the United States, Mexico, and the Caribbean. Each has its own languages, traditions, music, sports, and symbols. But the region shares a continent, shared histories, and cultures that move freely across borders. A good curator describes each one fairly AND shows what connects them.

🦉
🧭 Opti says…
One last curator tip: cultures don't stop at borders. A song born in Jamaica might be sung in Toronto next week; a recipe from Mexico might be loved in Chicago. When you compare regions, show what's distinct AND show what travels between them. That's a complete story.

You've compared the four panels. One last check before your final comparison.

🧠
Quick Self-Check
🧠

Not graded. Just for you! Answer these three questions before writing your final comparison.

1. Which country has TWO official languages, English and French?
ACanada
BMexico
CThe United States
Right! Canada has two official languages, English and French. Most people in the province of Quebec speak French.
Think about where French settlers landed long ago and where French is still widely spoken today.
2. The Day of the Dead and mariachi music are cultural characteristics of which region?
ACanada
BThe Caribbean
CMexico
Yes! Both the Day of the Dead and mariachi music come from Mexico. Both blend Indigenous and Spanish heritage.
Mariachi bands use trumpets and violins, and Día de Muertos is a colorful November holiday honoring relatives. Where do these come from?
3. What is one thing that CONNECTS the four regions of North America and the Caribbean?
AAll four regions speak only one language.
BMusic, food, and traditions move freely between the regions.
CThe four regions never trade with each other.
Exactly! Cultures don't stop at borders. A song from Jamaica might be popular in Toronto. A Mexican dish might be loved in Chicago. The regions are distinct AND connected.
The regions speak many different languages and trade together every day. What's something cultural that travels between them?

Curator Task: Final Comparison Panel
The label that earns you the Regional Observer badge.

Pick two of the four regional areas (Canada, the United States, Mexico, or the Caribbean). Write a 4-sentence comparison panel, one sentence for each of these:

  • One specific cultural characteristic of the first region
  • One specific cultural characteristic of the second region
  • One clear difference between them
  • One thing that connects them
Your 4 sentences help visitors see BOTH what makes each region distinct AND what links them together.
